title: What Terpenes Are, and Why Flavour Varies
summary: Terpenes are the volatile aromatic compounds that give plants their smell — limonene in citrus peel, pinene in pine, linalool in lavender. They are why two products with similar cannabinoid figures taste nothing alike, and because they evaporate easily, they are also the first thing heat and time take away.
body: Terpenes are not unique to any one plant. They are the aromatic compounds behind nearly every smell in the plant world, and they are the main reason two products can read almost identically on a certificate and taste completely different.
## The ones you will see named

| Terpene | Found in | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Limonene | Citrus peel | Bright, sharp, citrus |
| Pinene | Pine, rosemary | Sharp, resinous, forest |
| Myrcene | Hops, mango, thyme | Earthy, musky, herbal |
| Linalool | Lavender, coriander | Floral, soft, slightly spicy |
| Caryophyllene | Black pepper, cloves | Peppery, woody |
| Terpinolene | Nutmeg, apples | Fresh, faintly sweet |
| Humulene | Hops | Dry, hoppy, earthy |
A product's aroma is a blend of dozens, not one, and the proportions matter more than the presence of any single compound.
## Why they disappear

Terpenes are **volatile** — that is the defining property. They evaporate at temperatures far below where cannabinoids change, many of them below 70°C, and they oxidise on contact with air. Three consequences follow:

- **Heat strips flavour before it affects anything else.** A product stored warm loses its character first.
- **An opened container loses aroma steadily**, even sealed again.
- **The processing method decides how many survive.** Anything involving sustained heat keeps fewer.
That is the entire reason "live" products exist as a category. See [live resin, distillate, rosin and diamonds](/blog/live-resin-distillate-rosin-and-diamonds).
## Botanical versus retained

Two ways a product ends up tasting of something. Either the plant's own terpenes survived processing, or terpenes were removed and something was added back — often **botanical terpenes** from other plants, because limonene from an orange is the same molecule as limonene from anywhere else.

Neither is dishonest, and a certificate will not always tell you which happened. A terpene profile listing a dozen compounds in plausible proportions usually indicates retained plant terpenes; three compounds in round numbers usually indicates a blend added back.
## What terpene figures do not tell you

A terpene percentage describes aroma chemistry. It is not a strength figure, it is not a quality score, and no claim about what any of these compounds does in a body belongs on a label or in an article. If you see one making such a claim, that tells you something about the seller.
## Reading the figure

Total terpenes on a certificate typically run from a fraction of a per cent to a few per cent. Higher usually means less heat in processing and fresher material. Compare figures only between products tested by the same laboratory on the same panel, because methods differ. See [how cannabinoid figures are measured](/blog/how-a-total-thc-number-is-worked-out).

title: CBD, CBG, CBN and the Minor Cannabinoids
summary: Beyond the two best-known compounds sit dozens of others, present in much smaller amounts. CBG is the precursor the plant builds the rest from, CBN forms as material ages and oxidises, and CBC and THCV appear in traces. A certificate lists them because the panel measures them, not because any claim attaches.
body: A cannabinoid panel usually lists ten to sixteen compounds. Most are present in fractions of a per cent, and their names cause more confusion than their quantities justify.
## The list you will see

| Abbreviation | Name | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CBD | Cannabidiol | One of the two most abundant in most material |
| CBDA | Cannabidiolic acid | The acid form, before heat |
| CBG | Cannabigerol | The precursor the plant builds others from |
| CBGA | Cannabigerolic acid | Its acid form — the starting molecule |
| CBN | Cannabinol | Forms as material ages and oxidises |
| CBC | Cannabichromene | Usually a trace |
| THCV | Tetrahydrocannabivarin | Usually a trace |
| CBDV, CBL | Varin and cyclol forms | Traces, often below quantifiable levels |
## The acid forms and why they matter

Most cannabinoids exist in the living plant as **acids** — with an A on the end — and convert to the non-acid form when heated. That conversion is why a certificate reports both, and why the arithmetic on a total figure is not simple addition. See [THCa and what heat does to it](/blog/thca-and-what-heat-does-to-it).
## CBG, the precursor

CBGA is the molecule the plant's enzymes work on to make the others, which is why mature material usually shows very little of it left: most was converted during growth. Material harvested early, or bred for it, shows more.
## CBN, the age marker

CBN is the one worth understanding, because it is not really a feature — it is a clock. It forms as material oxidises, so an elevated CBN figure relative to what was reported at harvest indicates age, heat or air exposure somewhere in the chain.

A certificate showing a noticeable CBN figure on a product sold as fresh tells you something the marketing did not. See [what happens in heat, light and air](/blog/what-happens-in-heat-light-and-air).
## LOQ and ND

Two abbreviations that confuse people more than the cannabinoids do. **ND** means not detected. **LOQ** — limit of quantification — is the smallest amount the method can put a reliable number on; below it, a result reads "<LOQ" rather than zero. Most minor cannabinoids sit at or below it, which is normal rather than suspicious.
## What no article should tell you

What any of these compounds does in a body is a question for research and regulators, not for a product page. Nothing here is a claim of any effect or benefit, and a seller offering one about a minor cannabinoid is telling you to read everything else they say more carefully.

title: Full Spectrum, Broad Spectrum and Isolate
summary: Full spectrum keeps everything the plant produced. Broad spectrum keeps the rest but removes one or more compounds deliberately. Isolate is a single compound purified to 95 per cent and above, with nothing else left. The three are processing descriptions, not quality grades, and only a certificate confirms which you have.
body: Three terms that describe how much of the original plant chemistry survived processing. None is regulated, all three are used loosely, and the certificate is the only place the answer is not a matter of marketing.
## The three, plainly

| Term | What is present | What it looks like on a certificate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Full spectrum** | Everything the plant made, in roughly natural proportions | Many cannabinoids, a real terpene profile |
| **Broad spectrum** | Most of it, with specific compounds removed | Many cannabinoids, one at ND or <LOQ |
| **Isolate** | One compound, purified | One figure at 95%+, everything else ND |

The diagnostic is straightforward: a genuine broad spectrum product shows a full list of compounds **with a conspicuous gap**. If the whole list is empty except one line, that is an isolate whatever the box says.
## Where the terms get stretched

"Full spectrum" is the most abused of the three. Material that was processed hot, stripped of terpenes and then had a terpene blend added back is still sold that way, and on a certificate it reads as a short cannabinoid list with a suspiciously tidy three-terpene profile.

"Broad spectrum" sometimes means one compound was removed and sometimes means several were, and the label rarely says which. It is a claim about an absence, which is exactly the kind of claim a certificate is for.
## Isolate is a purity figure, not a quality one

An isolate at 99 per cent tells you what the other one per cent is not, and nothing about how it got there. Purity and cleanliness are different questions: a highly pure isolate made with solvents still needs a residual solvent panel before anyone should be satisfied with it. See [what a contaminant panel covers](/blog/what-a-contaminant-panel-actually-covers).
## Which to prefer
That depends on what you want, and the honest answer is that the words themselves should not decide it:

- Want the plant's own chemistry and flavour? Look for a **long cannabinoid list and a many-compound terpene profile**, not the phrase "full spectrum".
- Want one compound absent? Look for it at **ND on the certificate**, not for the phrase "broad spectrum".
- Want a single compound only? An **isolate with a residual solvent panel**.
In every case the certificate settles it and the label does not. See [why a test date matters as much as the number](/blog/why-a-test-date-matters-as-much-as-the-figure).

title: What Indica, Sativa and Hybrid Actually Tell You
summary: Almost nothing, at this point. The words began as botanical descriptions of plant shape and growing region, and generations of crossbreeding have made them commercial shorthand. Two products labelled the same way can have entirely different chemistry, which is why the certificate and the terpene profile are the useful information.
body: These are the most widely used words in the category and the least informative. It is worth knowing why, because they are on almost every box.
## What they originally described

Eighteenth and nineteenth-century botanists used the names for plants of different appearance and origin: one tall and narrow-leaved from warmer regions, one shorter and broad-leaved from further north. The distinction was about **morphology and provenance** — the shape of the plant and where it grew.
That is a description of a plant in a field. It was never a description of chemistry.
## Why the words drifted

Decades of deliberate crossbreeding mean that virtually everything commercially grown today is a hybrid of hybrids. The labels survived because they are useful to sell with, not because they still divide anything. A modern plant sold under either name may be genetically closer to something sold under the other.
"Hybrid" as a third category makes the problem visible: if nearly everything is a hybrid, the word carries no information at all.
## What varies instead

| Label | What it reliably tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Indica / sativa / hybrid | The seller's chosen shorthand |
| Strain name | Lineage as claimed — unregulated, frequently reused |
| Cannabinoid figures | Measured chemistry, if a certificate backs them |
| Terpene profile | Measured aroma chemistry — the closest thing to a fingerprint |

A terpene profile is the most honest description of a product available, because it is measured rather than asserted, and because it is what you actually notice. See [terpenes and why flavour varies](/blog/terpenes-and-why-flavour-varies).
## Strain names

Strain names are not administered by anyone. The same name is used by unrelated growers for unrelated plants, names are reused because they sell, and nothing stops anyone using any of them. Read as a rough indication of intended character they are harmless; treated as a specification they are misleading.
## What to do with a label instead

1. Ignore the three-word category.
2. Read the certificate for the batch code on the package.
3. Read the terpene profile — that is what you will taste.
4. Check the test date, and whether a contaminant panel was run.

And read any claim about what a category does in a body as marketing. Those claims are exactly what regulators cite, and they are not something this site will make. See [reading a product label](/blog/reading-a-label-line-by-line).

title: Live Resin, Distillate, Rosin and Diamonds
summary: Four words describing how a concentrate was made. Live resin is processed from fresh-frozen material to keep aroma compounds; distillate is refined with heat until one compound dominates; rosin is pressed with heat and pressure and no solvent; diamonds are crystallised cannabinoid acid, usually sitting in a sauce.
body: These four terms describe process, not grade. Knowing what each process does to the material tells you more than any of the adjectives on the packaging.
## The four

| Term | How it is made | What survives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Live resin** | Separated from fresh-frozen plant material with a solvent | Aroma compounds — the point of the format |
| **Distillate** | Refined under heat and vacuum until one compound dominates | Very little else; usually flavourless |
| **Rosin** | Heat and pressure only, no solvent | Aroma compounds, plus more plant material |
| **Diamonds** | Cannabinoid acid crystallised out of solution | The crystal is nearly one compound; the sauce holds the aroma |
## What "live" means

It refers to the starting material, not the finished product: plants frozen immediately after harvest instead of dried and cured. Because aroma compounds evaporate during drying, freezing keeps a great deal more of them. That is the whole claim, and it is a claim about handling before processing rather than about the process itself.
## Why distillate tastes of nothing

Refining under heat is very effective at isolating one compound and equally effective at removing everything volatile. A distillate is therefore usually flavourless, which is why products based on one have terpenes added back — sometimes the plant's own, often botanical ones from elsewhere. See [full spectrum, broad spectrum and isolate](/blog/full-spectrum-broad-spectrum-and-isolate-what-they-mean).
## Rosin, and what solventless costs

Rosin uses only heat and pressure, so there is no solvent to remove and nothing to test for in that respect. The trade-off is efficiency: pressing recovers less from the same material, which is why it costs more. See [what solventless actually means](/blog/what-solventless-actually-means).
## Diamonds and sauce

Left in solution under the right conditions, cannabinoid acid forms crystals — the "diamonds" — while the aromatic fraction stays liquid around them as "sauce". The crystal is close to a single compound; almost all the character is in the liquid. A jar of large diamonds in very little sauce looks impressive and tastes of less than the reverse.
Because the crystal is the **acid** form, heat changes it. See [THCa and what heat does to it](/blog/thca-and-what-heat-does-to-it).
## What none of these words is

None is a quality grade, none is regulated, and none tells you whether the material was clean. A solvent-extracted product needs a residual solvent panel; any concentrate concentrates whatever was on the plant, including what you would rather it did not. See [what a contaminant panel covers](/blog/what-a-contaminant-panel-actually-covers).

title: THCa and What Heat Does to It
summary: THCa is the acid form the living plant actually produces. Heat drives off a carbon dioxide group and converts it to the non-acid compound, losing about 12 per cent of the molecular weight in the process. That conversion is why a certificate reports both figures and why totals are calculated rather than added.
body: Almost every cannabinoid exists in the fresh plant as an acid, with an A on the end of its abbreviation. The non-acid forms people talk about are mostly products of heat and time, not of the plant.
## The conversion

Applying heat removes a carboxyl group from the molecule, which leaves as carbon dioxide. Chemists call it **decarboxylation**. The remaining molecule is lighter — the carboxyl group accounts for roughly 12.3 per cent of the original mass — which is where the conversion factor in every total calculation comes from.

| Property | Acid form | After heat |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Present in | Fresh and dried plant material | Heated material, aged material |
| Mass | Higher | About 87.7% of the acid's |
| On a certificate | Reported separately | Reported separately |
## Why the arithmetic is not addition
Because one converts into the other with a loss of mass, adding the two figures overstates what the material can become. A total is calculated instead:
**total = (acid figure × 0.877) + non-acid figure**

The 0.877 is the mass ratio described above. Adding the raw numbers instead produces a figure roughly 12 per cent too high, which is a common way potency claims are inflated without anything being technically fabricated. See [how a total figure is worked out](/blog/how-a-total-thc-number-is-worked-out).
## What causes the conversion in practice

- **Deliberate heat** in processing.
- **Time**, slowly, at room temperature.
- **Warm storage**, faster — a hot car does in days what a cool cupboard does in months.
- **Light**, which also drives oxidation to other compounds entirely.

This is why a certificate is a snapshot of a batch on a date rather than a permanent description, and why the date on it matters as much as the figures. See [what happens in heat, light and air](/blog/what-happens-in-heat-light-and-air).
## Crystals

The crystalline material sold as "diamonds" is usually the acid form, which is what crystallises cleanly. Heating it converts it in the same way as anything else. See [live resin, distillate, rosin and diamonds](/blog/live-resin-distillate-rosin-and-diamonds).
## On regulatory figures

Thresholds written into law are defined in statute, and both the numbers and the way the total is calculated have been revisited by legislators more than once. Nothing on this page is legal advice, and an article is the wrong place to learn the current rule — read the statute or ask a lawyer who works in the field. What an article can tell you is the chemistry, which does not change.

title: How a Total Figure on a Certificate Is Worked Out
summary: A total is calculated, not added: the acid figure is multiplied by 0.877 to account for mass lost on conversion, then the non-acid figure is added. Adding the two raw numbers instead inflates the result by about 12 per cent, which is the most common way a legitimate certificate is misread.
body: Two products can carry certificates from the same laboratory and advertise very different figures from almost identical data, purely because of how the total was worked out.
## The formula
**Total = (acid form × 0.877) + non-acid form**

The multiplier exists because the acid loses a carboxyl group when it converts, and that group is about 12.3 per cent of the molecule's mass. The conversion cannot produce more than 87.7 per cent of the acid's weight, so a total that ignores it describes something chemically impossible. See [THCa and what heat does to it](/blog/thca-and-what-heat-does-to-it).
## Worked through

| Reported on the certificate | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| Acid form | 20.0% |
| Non-acid form | 0.8% |
| **Correct total** | (20.0 × 0.877) + 0.8 = **18.3%** |
| Wrong total, simple addition | 20.8% |
A 2.5 point difference from arithmetic alone. On a shelf beside competitors, that is exactly the sort of gap that decides a purchase.
## How to check one yourself

1. Find the acid figure and the non-acid figure as separate lines. A certificate that reports only a total is hiding the step you want to check.
2. Multiply the acid figure by 0.877.
3. Add the non-acid figure.
4. Compare with what the packaging claims.
If the package figure is meaningfully higher than your calculation, the difference is usually the missing multiplier.
## Other ways figures drift apart

- **Dry weight versus as-received.** A moist sample reported as-received gives a lower percentage than the same material reported on a dry basis. The certificate states which.
- **Per unit versus per gram.** Milligrams per unit and percentage by weight are different measurements; converting between them needs the unit's weight.
- **Rounding at each step**, which is minor but always in the seller's favour.
- **A different laboratory.** Two accredited laboratories testing the same sample can differ by a point or more. See [how cannabinoid figures are measured](/blog/how-cannabinoid-figures-are-measured).
## Why the figure is not the interesting part

A potency figure describes one batch on one date and says nothing about whether the material was clean. The contaminant panel is the part worth reading, and it is the part most certificates published for marketing purposes leave out. See [what a full contaminant panel covers](/blog/what-a-contaminant-panel-actually-covers).

title: What Solventless Actually Means
summary: Solventless means the material was separated using only water, ice, heat, pressure or agitation — no butane, propane, ethanol or carbon dioxide at any stage. It is not a synonym for clean or for strong. It removes one category of risk, and every other question about contamination still applies.
body: A useful term, and one that is regularly stretched to mean more than it does.
## Solventless and solvent-free are not the same claim
**Solventless** describes the process: no chemical solvent was used to separate anything.
**Solvent-free** describes the result: a solvent was used and the residue is below some threshold.

The second is a much weaker statement and is often printed where the first is implied. A certificate's residual solvent panel is what distinguishes them — on genuinely solventless material there is nothing for that panel to find.
## What counts as solventless

| Method | How it separates | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heat and pressure | Presses material between heated plates | Rosin |
| Ice water and agitation | Aroma glands separate and are sieved out | Hash, then pressed rosin |
| Dry sieving | Mechanical separation through screens | Sift |
Water is technically a solvent, and the convention in this trade is that water and ice do not count as one. That is a convention, not a definition anyone administers.
## What it does not tell you

- **Not cleaner by default.** Anything on the plant — pesticide residue, heavy metals taken up from soil, mould — concentrates along with everything else. Pressing does not remove contaminants; it concentrates them.
- **Not stronger.** Solventless products are often lower in a headline figure than a distillate, because less was stripped away.
- **Not automatically better tasting**, though it usually keeps more aroma than a hot process does. See [terpenes and why flavour varies](/blog/terpenes-and-why-flavour-varies).
## Why it costs more

Pressing and ice-water separation recover less from the same weight of plant material than a solvent process does, and both need better starting material to be worth doing. The price difference is mostly about efficiency, not about marketing.
## What to check instead of the word

1. **A residual solvent panel**, even on a solventless claim — its absence of findings is the evidence.
2. **A contaminant panel**, because concentration cuts both ways. See [what a full contaminant panel covers](/blog/what-a-contaminant-panel-actually-covers).
3. **The batch code**, matching the package in your hand.
4. **The test date.**
A product described as solventless with no certificate at all has told you nothing verifiable. See [live resin, distillate, rosin and diamonds](/blog/live-resin-distillate-rosin-and-diamonds).

title: What Happens in Heat, Light and Air
summary: Three things degrade a product and they act at different speeds: light drives oxidation fastest, heat accelerates every reaction including conversion of acid forms, and air supplies the oxygen. Aroma goes first, colour darkens next, and the cannabinoid profile shifts last. Cool, dark and sealed is the whole answer.
body: A certificate describes a batch on a date. What happens between that date and the moment you use it is decided by three variables, and by how the product was stored rather than by who sold it.
## What each one does

| Factor | Effect | Speed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Light**, especially UV | Drives oxidation; breaks compounds down | Fastest — a sunny windowsill works in days |
| **Heat** | Accelerates every reaction, including acid conversion | Fast above about 30°C |
| **Air** | Supplies oxygen for oxidation; carries aroma away | Steady once opened |
| **Time** alone, cool and dark | Slow drift | Months to years |
## The order things change in

1. **Aroma.** Terpenes are volatile and go first, often before anything else is noticeable. A product that smells of less than it did has already changed. See [terpenes and why flavour varies](/blog/terpenes-and-why-flavour-varies).
2. **Colour.** Oxidation darkens most concentrates — pale gold towards amber, amber towards brown. Darkening alone is not spoilage, but it is a reliable clock.
3. **Thickness.** Oxidised material is usually thicker, which shows up as a cartridge that draws harder than it did.
4. **The cannabinoid profile.** Acid forms convert; some compounds oxidise to others. A rising CBN figure is the classic age marker. See [CBD, CBG, CBN and the minor cannabinoids](/blog/the-minor-cannabinoids-cbd-cbg-and-cbn).
## What good storage looks like

- **Cool.** Room temperature or below; never a car, a windowsill or on top of anything with a motor in it.
- **Dark.** A drawer or a box. Tinted packaging helps and is not a substitute for a dark cupboard.
- **Sealed.** Air exchange is what oxidation needs. Close it properly every time.
- **Upright**, for anything in a cartridge. See [storing a device](/blog/storing-a-device-heat-light-and-which-way-up).
- **Stable.** Repeated warming and cooling is worse than a steady slightly-too-warm cupboard, because each cycle moves air in and out.
## Refrigeration

Usually not worth it and sometimes harmful. Cold thickens contents, which makes a cartridge behave badly, and moving a cold container into a warm room draws condensation inside it. A cool dark cupboard beats a fridge for almost everything here.
## Reading a certificate with age in mind

This is why a test date is not a formality. A figure measured eighteen months ago describes material that has since been through a summer, a supply chain and a shelf. The number was true; it is no longer a description of what you hold. See [why a test date matters as much as the figure](/blog/why-a-test-date-matters-as-much-as-the-figure).

title: What ISO 17025 Accreditation Means
summary: ISO/IEC 17025 is the international standard for testing laboratory competence. An accredited laboratory has been assessed by an outside body on its methods, equipment calibration, staff and record keeping, for the specific tests it is accredited to run. It is the difference between a laboratory and a room with instruments in it.
body: Anyone can buy an instrument, run a sample and print a report on headed paper. Accreditation is the mechanism that separates that from a laboratory whose numbers mean something.
## What the standard covers

ISO/IEC 17025 is published jointly by the International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission, and it is the standard against which testing and calibration laboratories worldwide are assessed. An assessment looks at:

- **Methods** — validated, documented, and appropriate for the material.
- **Equipment** — calibrated against traceable references on a schedule.
- **Staff** — trained and assessed as competent for the tests they run.
- **Sample handling** — chain of custody from arrival to disposal.
- **Records** — every result reproducible from what was kept.
- **Uncertainty** — the laboratory knows and states how precise its figures are.
## Accreditation is scoped

The part most people miss. A laboratory is accredited **for specific tests**, not in general. A laboratory accredited for potency is not thereby accredited for heavy metals, and its heavy-metal report carries no accreditation at all even though the letterhead is the same.
The scope is published by the accreditation body. If a certificate matters to you, the scope document is what to check.
## Who accredits

In the United States the recognised bodies include A2LA, ANAB and Perry Johnson Laboratory Accreditation; internationally, the members of the ILAC mutual recognition arrangement. Each publishes a searchable directory of the laboratories it accredits and what for.
A logo on a report is not accreditation. The directory entry is.
## What it is not

| Not | Because |
| --- | --- |
| A guarantee the product is good | It certifies the laboratory, not the sample |
| A licence | Licensing is a state matter, separate from accreditation |
| Permanent | It is reassessed, and it can lapse |
| Whole-laboratory | It applies only within the accredited scope |
## How to check one in five minutes

1. Take the laboratory's name from the certificate.
2. Find the accreditation body named on it.
3. Search that body's public directory for the laboratory.
4. Open the scope and confirm the tests on your certificate are in it.
5. Check the accreditation has not expired.
If the laboratory is not listed, the report is one company's word. That may still be true — it is simply not evidence. See [a glossary of certificate terms](/blog/a-glossary-of-certificate-terms).

title: What a Full Contaminant Panel Covers
summary: Five families of test: heavy metals, pesticides, residual solvents, microbials and mycotoxins, plus water activity on plant material. Potency is not a safety test and appears on nearly every certificate published for marketing, while the panels that matter are the ones most often missing.
body: A certificate showing only cannabinoid figures is telling you the least useful thing a laboratory can measure. The safety information is in the panels beside it.
## The five families

| Panel | What it looks for | Why it is there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Heavy metals** | Lead, arsenic, cadmium, mercury | Taken up from soil and water; also from hardware |
| **Pesticides** | Dozens of named compounds | Applied during growing; concentrate with everything else |
| **Residual solvents** | Butane, propane, ethanol, hexane and others | Left behind by a solvent process |
| **Microbials** | Total counts, E. coli, salmonella, Aspergillus species | Growing and handling conditions |
| **Mycotoxins** | Aflatoxins, ochratoxin A | Produced by moulds, and not removed by processing |
On plant material, **water activity** or moisture content belongs beside them, because it predicts whether mould can develop after testing.
## Why concentration cuts both ways

Any process that concentrates the material concentrates what was on it. A pesticide residue at an unremarkable level on a plant can end up at a multiple of that in a concentrate made from it. This is why a contaminant panel on a concentrate is more important than on the raw material, not less.
## The four heavy metals, and hardware

The standard four are lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury. Lead deserves particular attention on anything sold in a cartridge, because it can migrate from the hardware itself rather than from the plant — a metal component, a solder joint, a cheap alloy. A potency-only certificate for a cartridge leaves that question entirely unanswered.
## What "pass" means

Nothing, by itself. A pass is measured against an **action limit**, and those limits are set by state regulation and differ from state to state. A result that passes in one jurisdiction can fail in another, so a certificate reporting measured values is more useful than one reporting only pass or fail.
## Reading the abbreviations

**ND** — not detected. **<LOQ** — present below the level the method can quantify reliably. **LOD** — the smallest amount detectable at all. A column of ND results is the good outcome, and a column of numbers is not automatically a bad one — it depends on the limits.
## What to ask for

The full panel for the batch code printed on your package, not a sample certificate for the product line. If a seller can produce a potency figure but not a contaminant panel, that is the answer to your question. See [what a batch code is for](/blog/what-a-batch-code-is-for) and [why potency belongs on a certificate](/blog/why-potency-belongs-on-a-certificate).

title: What a Batch Code Is For
summary: A batch code identifies one production run, and it is the only thing tying a certificate to the package in your hand. A genuine report for a different batch describes material you do not have — which is the most common way an honest-looking certificate turns out to be irrelevant.
body: Of everything printed on a package, the batch code is the piece that makes the rest checkable.
## What it identifies

One run: material processed together, filled together, tested together. Everything a certificate reports applies to that run and to nothing else. A second run of the same recipe a month later is a different batch with different figures, however identical the packaging.
## Why a mismatch matters more than a missing report

This is the failure mode worth understanding. Someone asks for a certificate, receives a real one from a real accredited laboratory, reads it carefully — and it is for batch 2411-A while the jar says 2502-C. Nothing was forged. It simply describes different material.

| Situation | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Code on package matches certificate | The report describes what you hold |
| Codes differ | The report describes something else |
| No code on the package | Nothing can be verified at all |
| Code present, no certificate available | The seller can be asked; a refusal is informative |
## What codes look like

There is no standard. Common patterns encode a date — 2502 for February 2025, or a Julian day — plus a line or run letter. Some are sequential with no meaning at all. The format does not matter; the **match** does.
## Where to find it

On the label, stamped into the base, printed on a foil seal, or inside a folded insert. On small hardware it is often on the shrink wrap, which is the argument for not throwing the wrap away until you have checked.
## Using one

1. Find the code on the package.
2. Ask the seller for the certificate **for that code**, or look it up if they publish by batch.
3. Confirm the code on the report matches exactly.
4. Check the test date. See [why a test date matters as much as the figure](/blog/why-a-test-date-matters-as-much-as-the-figure).
5. Read the panels, not just the headline figure. See [what a full contaminant panel covers](/blog/what-a-contaminant-panel-actually-covers).
## What a batch code also enables

Recalls. Without one, a problem found in one run cannot be traced to the packages that came from it, so the only options are recalling everything or nothing. A seller who codes by batch can answer a question about a specific jar; one who does not cannot, whatever their intentions.

title: Why a Test Date Matters as Much as the Figure
summary: A certificate is a photograph, not a description. It records what a sample contained on one date, and material changes with heat, light, air and time. A two-year-old report for a product bought today was accurate when written and is no longer a statement about what is in the package.
body: Two dates appear on most certificates and they are not the same: the date the sample was received, and the date it was analysed. Either is more informative than the figures if the gap to today is large.
## What changes after testing

| What | Direction |
| --- | --- |
| Aroma compounds | Down, fastest of all |
| Acid forms of cannabinoids | Convert, gradually |
| Oxidation markers such as CBN | Up |
| Moisture on plant material | Either way, with storage |
| Microbial counts | Up, if moisture allowed it |
None of this is a defect. It is what organic material does. See [what happens in heat, light and air](/blog/what-happens-in-heat-light-and-air).
## What an old report tells you about the seller

More than it tells you about the product. A report from two years ago on a current product usually means one of three things: the batch is old, the product line is tested rarely and the same report is reused, or nobody has looked at it since it was filed. All three are information.
The same applies to a certificate with the batch code removed or illegible. See [what a batch code is for](/blog/what-a-batch-code-is-for).
## A rough guide

- **Under six months** — current; figures are a fair description.
- **Six to twelve months** — usable; expect aroma to have faded.
- **Over a year** — read the potency figure as historic; the contaminant panel is still largely informative, because heavy metals and pesticide residues do not go away.
- **No date at all** — not a certificate. A report without a date cannot be checked against anything.
That last distinction is worth keeping: age erodes the potency figures much faster than it erodes the safety panels.
## Microbial results are the exception

A microbial panel is the most perishable result on the page, because it describes a population that can grow. On plant material stored with too much moisture, a clean microbial result from a year ago says very little about today. Water activity, where reported, is what indicates whether growth was possible.
## The two questions to ask

Which batch, and when was it tested. Everything else on a certificate is easier to interpret once those two are answered, and a seller who cannot answer them is not withholding detail — they are telling you the chain does not exist. See [what ISO 17025 accreditation means](/blog/what-iso-17025-accreditation-means).

title: Why Potency Belongs on a Certificate, Not a Box
summary: A figure printed on packaging is a marketing claim fixed at design time; a figure on a batch certificate is a measurement of what was in the material. Packaging is printed in bulk before the batch exists, so a printed number describes an intention rather than a result.
body: The argument is not that printed figures are dishonest. It is that they cannot be accurate in the way people read them.
## Why a printed figure cannot be a measurement

Packaging is designed once and printed in the thousands, often months before a given batch is made. Whatever number is on it was chosen before the material existed. Batches vary — the same recipe and the same source give different figures run to run — so a printed number is a target, a rounding, or a category average.
A certificate is generated after the fact from a sample of one run. That is the difference: one is an intention, the other is a result.
## What varies between batches

| Source of variation | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Different starting material | Sometimes points, not fractions |
| Processing run to run | Small but real |
| Time between manufacture and testing | Acid forms convert |
| Sampling within a batch | Real, which is why sampling method is reported |
| Laboratory to laboratory | Can exceed a point on the same sample |
## How a legitimate printed figure is arrived at

Usually one of three ways, none of which is a lie and none of which is a measurement of your unit: a rounded figure from an earlier batch; a minimum the producer expects to exceed; or a formulation target. Read a printed number as "about this much, by design".
## The arithmetic problem on top

Even where a printed figure comes from real data, the way a total is calculated can inflate it by about 12 per cent if the conversion factor is left out. That is an arithmetic choice made once at design time and reprinted thousands of times. See [how a total figure is worked out](/blog/how-a-total-thc-number-is-worked-out).
## What to do with the box

Use it for what it is good for: the batch code, the net weight, the ingredient list, the manufacturer's identity. Then take the batch code to the certificate for the figures. See [reading a label line by line](/blog/reading-a-label-line-by-line).
## And what a figure never tells you

Whether the material was clean. A potency number is not a safety test, and a certificate published without a contaminant panel has answered the least important question at length. See [what a full contaminant panel covers](/blog/what-a-contaminant-panel-actually-covers).

title: Reading a Product Label, Line by Line
summary: Six things on a label are checkable and the rest is presentation: the manufacturer's identity and address, the net weight or volume, the ingredient list, the batch code, any date, and the warnings. Everything else — the strain name, the category word, the headline figure — is chosen by whoever designed the box.
body: A label does two jobs at once: it sells, and it identifies. The identifying parts are small, dull and useful; the selling parts are large and mostly unverifiable.
## The six checkable lines

| Line | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| **Manufacturer and address** | A real named company and a real address, not just a brand |
| **Net weight or volume** | A specific figure with units, not "full gram" as a style |
| **Ingredients** | In descending order; additives named rather than implied |
| **Batch code** | Present and legible — the key to everything else |
| **Date** | Manufacture, test or best-before; any of them helps |
| **Warnings** | Present. Absence is a sign of a producer cutting corners |
A brand name with no company behind it is the most common omission and the most telling one. If something goes wrong there is nobody named to contact, which is sometimes the point.
## The parts that sell rather than inform

- **Strain names** are unregulated and reused freely by unrelated producers.
- **Category words** — the three-way indica, sativa, hybrid split — no longer divide anything reliably. See [what indica, sativa and hybrid actually tell you](/blog/what-indica-sativa-and-hybrid-actually-tell-you).
- **Headline figures** are printed before the batch exists. See [why potency belongs on a certificate](/blog/why-potency-belongs-on-a-certificate).
- **"Lab tested"** with no batch code and no report is a phrase, not a fact.
- **"Premium", "artisan", "small batch"** mean nothing in particular.
## Ingredient lists worth a second look

Two patterns are worth noticing. A list ending in "natural flavours" or "botanical terpenes" indicates flavour was added rather than retained — not a fault, just useful to know. And a very short list on a product described as full spectrum is a contradiction the certificate will settle. See [full spectrum, broad spectrum and isolate](/blog/full-spectrum-broad-spectrum-and-isolate-what-they-mean).
## The QR code

Scan it, and then check where it went. A QR code that opens a marketing page, a product line certificate, or a dated report for a different batch is common. One that opens the certificate for the batch code on your package is the thing it is supposed to be. See [what a batch code is for](/blog/what-a-batch-code-is-for).
## A two-minute routine

1. Find the manufacturer's name and address.
2. Find the batch code and keep the wrap until you have.
3. Scan or request the certificate for that code.
4. Check the test date.
5. Read the contaminant panels before the potency figure.
6. Check the arithmetic on any total. See [how a total figure is worked out](/blog/how-a-total-thc-number-is-worked-out).

title: Spotting Counterfeit Hardware
summary: Counterfeits copy the artwork and not the engineering. Look for misaligned or low-resolution printing, a missing or generic batch code, no working certificate lookup, unusually light weight, rough threads, and a price far below the market. Any one of these is a question; two together is an answer.
body: Counterfeit hardware is a real problem because the economics favour it: artwork is cheap to copy, and engineering is not. The tells are almost always in the manufacturing rather than the graphics.
## The physical tells

| Check | What a counterfeit usually shows |
| --- | --- |
| Print quality | Slightly soft edges, wrong shade, misaligned panels |
| Weight | Lighter — thinner metal, smaller cell |
| Threads | Rough, tight, or cross-threading easily |
| Seams and seals | Visible gaps, glue, an untidy join at the base |
| Mouthpiece fit | Loose, or a different plastic from the body |
| Font | Close but not identical to the brand's own |
Weight is the most reliable of these if you have ever held a genuine one. Counterfeits save money on the parts you cannot see.
## The paperwork tells

- **No batch code**, or a code that is the same on every unit in a display box.
- **A QR code that goes nowhere**, to a marketing page, or to a report whose code does not match yours.
- **A certificate that is an image**, not a report — a photograph of a document, with no laboratory name you can look up.
- **A laboratory that is not in any accreditation directory.** See [what ISO 17025 accreditation means](/blog/what-iso-17025-accreditation-means).
## Price

A price well below everyone else's is the most consistent signal of all. Manufacturing, testing and accreditation cost money; a unit priced below what the parts and the panel cost has saved that money somewhere.
## Why it matters beyond being cheated

The parts you cannot see are the parts that matter. Lead can migrate into contents from cheap alloys and solder joints, which is exactly what the heavy-metal panel on a certificate exists to catch — and a counterfeit has no certificate that applies to it. An unbranded lithium cell with minimal protection circuitry is the other half of the risk. See [charging a rechargeable device safely](/blog/charging-a-rechargeable-device-safely).
## If you already have one

Do not use it. Do not charge it. Tape over the port, keep it away from anything flammable, and take it to a battery collection point rather than a bin. See [disposing of hardware and lithium batteries](/blog/disposing-of-hardware-and-lithium-batteries).
## The single best defence

Buy where the batch code resolves to a certificate for that code. A seller who can produce the report for the package in your hand is a seller with a real chain behind them, and that chain is what a counterfeit cannot copy. See [what a batch code is for](/blog/what-a-batch-code-is-for).

title: How Cannabinoid Figures Are Measured
summary: A sample is homogenised, the compounds are dissolved out with a solvent, and the mixture is separated by chromatography — usually HPLC, which does not heat the sample and so can report acid and non-acid forms separately. Results are then compared against calibrated reference standards.
body: Knowing roughly how the figure was produced explains most of the odd things about certificates: why two laboratories disagree, why a total is calculated rather than added, and why sampling gets its own line on the report.
## The steps

1. **Sampling.** A portion is taken from the batch. How it was taken matters enormously, because a single grab from one corner does not represent a run.
2. **Homogenisation.** The sample is ground or mixed so it is uniform. Uneven material is the largest source of disagreement between laboratories.
3. **Preparation.** The compounds of interest are dissolved out with a solvent and diluted to a workable concentration.
4. **Separation.** The mixture is pushed through a chromatography column, which separates compounds by how strongly they interact with it.
5. **Detection and quantification.** A detector measures each compound as it emerges, and the result is compared against reference standards of known concentration.
## HPLC and GC

| Method | How it works | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **HPLC** — high performance liquid chromatography | Liquid solvent, no heat | Reports acid and non-acid forms **separately** |
| **GC** — gas chromatography | The sample is vaporised | Heat converts acid forms, so it reports a combined figure |

This is the single most useful thing to know about testing methods. A laboratory using HPLC can tell you how much acid form was present; one using GC cannot, because the instrument itself performs the conversion. It is also why the total on a certificate is calculated with a factor rather than added. See [THCa and what heat does to it](/blog/thca-and-what-heat-does-to-it).
GC coupled to mass spectrometry is standard for residual solvents, where vaporising the sample is exactly what you want.
## Why two laboratories differ
Differences of a point or more on the same material are routine and usually legitimate:

- **Sampling** — different portions of a non-uniform batch.
- **Preparation** — solvent choice and dilution.
- **Calibration** — different reference standards, each with its own uncertainty.
- **Reporting basis** — dry weight or as received.
- **Rounding** at each step.
A good certificate states its measurement uncertainty, which is the laboratory telling you how much of that spread it expects.
## What this means for a buyer

Compare figures only between certificates from the same laboratory on the same basis, take small differences as noise, and read the panels rather than ranking products by a decimal place. See [what a full contaminant panel covers](/blog/what-a-contaminant-panel-actually-covers) and [a glossary of certificate terms](/blog/a-glossary-of-certificate-terms).

title: A Glossary of Certificate Terms
summary: COA, LOD, LOQ, ND, action limit, dry weight basis, measurement uncertainty, chain of custody, homogenisation, accreditation scope. Twenty terms cover almost everything printed on a laboratory report, and knowing them turns a page of jargon into something you can actually check.
body: Laboratory reports are written for regulators and other laboratories, which is why they read the way they do. The vocabulary is small.
## The document

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **COA** | Certificate of analysis — the report for one sample from one batch |
| **Batch or lot** | One production run; everything on the report applies only to it |
| **Sample ID** | The laboratory's own reference for the portion tested |
| **Date received / date analysed** | Two different dates. The gap between them, and to today, both matter |
| **Chain of custody** | The documented handling record from collection to analysis |
| **Sampling method** | How the portion was taken. Whether it represents the batch depends on this |
## Limits and results

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **ND** | Not detected — below the detection limit |
| **LOD** | Limit of detection: the smallest amount the method can see at all |
| **LOQ** | Limit of quantification: the smallest amount it can put a reliable number on |
| **< LOQ** | Present, but too little to quantify. Not the same as zero |
| **Action limit** | The regulatory threshold a result is compared against. Set by state, so it varies |
| **Pass / fail** | Measured against the action limit — meaningless without knowing which |
| **Measurement uncertainty** | The range the true value sits in. Its presence is a good sign |
## Basis and units

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Dry weight basis** | Moisture removed from the calculation. Gives a higher percentage |
| **As received** | Reported on the sample as it arrived, moisture included |
| **mg/g** | Milligrams per gram. Divide by ten for a percentage |
| **mg per unit** | Total in one item. Needs the unit's weight to convert to a percentage |
| **ppm / ppb** | Parts per million or billion, used for contaminants |
| **Homogenisation** | Mixing the sample uniform before testing |
## The laboratory

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **ISO/IEC 17025** | The international standard for testing laboratory competence |
| **Accreditation scope** | The specific tests a laboratory is accredited for — not all of them |
| **Reference standard** | A material of known concentration used to calibrate |
| **Method blank** | A run with no sample, to confirm the equipment is not contributing |
## Two habits worth keeping

**Read the panels before the potency.** The interesting information is in what was tested for and not found. See [what a full contaminant panel covers](/blog/what-a-contaminant-panel-actually-covers).

**Check the batch code and the date first.** If either fails, nothing else on the page is about the package in your hand. See [what a batch code is for](/blog/what-a-batch-code-is-for) and [why a test date matters as much as the figure](/blog/why-a-test-date-matters-as-much-as-the-figure).
